summary.summary: Spelthorne's 2024/25 outturn shows a council carrying £1,069-1,072m of debt built almost entirely to fund a £583.1m commercial office-investment portfolio whose value has fallen 43% since acquisition. Financing costs consumed 315% of the council's own net revenue stream before investment-property income is netted off, and even netting that income in, the ratio (83%) remains far above the sub-18% typical of comparable authorities — one of the reasons the Secretary of State issued the Council with Statutory Directions on 8 May 2025 requiring an Improvement and Recovery Plan covering asset rationalisation and a strict debt-reduction plan. The council is also drawing down its investment-property Sinking Fund reserves (a budgeted £5.052m net withdrawal in 2025/26) to keep subsidising services, and its loans to its own housing/regeneration companies grew to £47.157m. Investable cash on hand (£10.9m plus cash balances averaging £9m) is thin against the £1bn+ debt stock.

signals.headline: Affordability indicator (financing costs/net revenue stream) hit 315% in the 2024/25 outturn, rated Red ('exceeds PI significantly') in the council's own RAG table; even net of investment-property income it is 83%, versus a sub-18% benchmark the council cites for comparable authorities.
signals.why: A financing-cost burden this far outside normal prudential ranges signals the debt/asset base is not sustainable on the council's own numbers.

signals.headline: Total capital financing costs rose to £44.7m in the 2024/25 outturn, against £36.6m budgeted (and £36.6m in 2023/24), while the underlying net revenue stream was just £14.2m.
signals.why: Financing costs are growing faster than the small revenue base that has to absorb them.

signals.headline: The 2025/26 budget assumes a net £5.052m withdrawal from investment-property Sinking Fund reserves, after a reserves-modelling refresh found balances need rebuilding by 2036.
signals.why: The council is spending down the very reserve set aside to smooth the commercial-property risk it is now suffering from.

signals.headline: Loans to the council's two wholly-owned companies rose to £47.157m at 31 March 2025 (from £32.517m a year earlier), including £44.449m to Knowle Green Estates Ltd at 3.37% plus a £2.5m interest-free debenture.
signals.why: Growing related-party lending is additional exposure sitting outside the headline PWLB debt figures.

signals.headline: Investment funds of just £10.9m (plus cash averaging £9m) are held against total borrowing of £1,069-1,072m at 31 March 2025.
signals.why: A very thin liquid buffer relative to the scale of the debt book leaves little room to absorb shocks.

news_drafts.headline: Spelthorne audit improves but improvement plan stalls on execution
news_drafts.lead: Spelthorne Council received a full audit assurance opinion for 2025-26, marking significant recovery after years of disclaimed audits, though the council remains under Secretary of State's Best Value Directions following governance failures. The council's internal controls are now deemed reasonable and functioning in practice, and external audit recognised improvement in financial reporting. However, an audit of the Improvement and Recovery Plan in April found significant control gaps, with 11 of 12 agreed management actions still pending four months later. The audit committee also added an unscheduled review of the Housing Savings Delivery Plan, approved in June, to examine the governance of savings assumptions underpinning the plan — suggesting concerns about the adequacy of controls over material forecasts as the council works towards its transition to West Surrey unitary authority.

news_drafts.headline: Spelthorne clears audit backlog but lags on recovery plan delivery
news_drafts.lead: Spelthorne's Audit Committee heard that the council has ended a seven-year audit backlog following government intervention. External auditors had disclaimed their opinions on the 2018 to 2024 accounts due to delays; the 2024-25 audit opinion was also disclaimed because opening balances could not be verified. However, the external auditors now recognise "positive trajectory" in financial reporting. Internal audit issued a full "reasonable assurance" opinion for 2025-26, indicating controls are functioning. The improvement follows a Best Value Inspection that triggered a governance reform programme, including revised audit committee procedures and a new Governance Assurance Framework. An independent review found the audit committee is now discharging its core responsibilities effectively. However, an April 2026 audit of the council's Improvement and Recovery Plan found significant control gaps, with 11 of 12 management actions still pending four months later. The council is preparing for transition to the West Surrey unitary authority.

findings.paper_title: Governance Assurance Report - Audit Committee 24 Sept 2026
findings.headline: Transition to new unitary council structure is a formal governance priority area.
findings.detail: One of the six Governance Assurance Areas under review is ensuring that programme and change management arrangements are effective to support the council's transition to a new unitary authority structure. The council is actively managing this major organizational restructuring within its governance framework.
findings.matters: Major structural reorganizations create operational complexity and financial risk; a lender would need confidence that transition management is effective, since service disruption or integration failures could affect the council's financial performance and ability to meet borrowing obligations.
findings.figures: Unitary transition: one of six governance areas under detailed review
findings.quote: Ensuring our programme and change management arrangements are effective to support the successful transition to the new unitary council

findings.paper_title: Governance Assurance Report - Audit Committee 24 Sept 2026
findings.headline: Governance assurance levels show no change since new framework implementation began in July.
findings.detail: The paper reports that overall assurance levels for the 12 Governance Assurance Areas remain unchanged since the Committee last met on 23 July, when the new governance framework was still being rolled out. This suggests the new approach has not yet produced measurable improvements in the council's risk position.
findings.matters: A lender would expect governance improvements to translate into measurable risk reduction over time; unchanged assurance levels indicate the council's governance-related risk profile has not shifted despite the framework redesign, raising questions about implementation effectiveness.
findings.figures: No changes to overall assurance level recorded since 23 July 2026
findings.quote: There are no changes to the overall level of assurance for the GAAs since last presented to the Committee on 23 July.

findings.paper_title: Governance Assurance Report - Audit Committee 24 Sept 2026
findings.headline: Council implementing governance overhaul following external audit recommendations from Best Value Inspection and Grant Thornton.
findings.detail: Spelthorne is replacing its Corporate Risk Register with a new Governance Assurance Register monitoring 12 key governance areas. The change was made in response to recommendations from a Best Value Inspection and Grant Thornton's External Audit. The Council is shifting to a governance assurance-based approach designed to embed risk management more effectively across the organization.
findings.matters: External audit recommendations indicate governance or control issues were identified; a council's responsive framework changes and willingness to embed improvements matter to lenders assessing governance quality, though the specific weaknesses flagged are not disclosed in this paper.
findings.figures: 12 Governance Assurance Areas; six being reviewed at this meeting
findings.quote: In response to recommendations made in the Best Value Inspection and Grant Thornton's External Audit of this authority, the Council has been improving its risk management arrangements, moving to a new Governance Assurance-based approach.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - 5 GAAs for Audit Committee 24.09.26
findings.headline: Environmental Health workload capacity strained by HMO regulation and 1 May Renter's Rights Bill implementation
findings.detail: Service flagged as Amber for workload management, specifically noting: 'Workload capacity is an issue particularly in relation to HMOs and the introduction of the Renter's Rights Bill on 1 May.' This is a statutory obligation with no flexibility.
findings.matters: Regulatory non-compliance carries legal and reputational risk. Inability to enforce new housing rights legislation affects both service users and reputation.
findings.quote: Workload capacity is an issue particularly in relation to HMOs and the introduction of the Renter's Rights Bill on 1 May.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - 5 GAAs for Audit Committee 24.09.26
findings.headline: Procurement KPI revision delayed by several months, reducing time available for corrective action on emerging problems
findings.detail: Fundamental review of procurement KPIs completed and approved May 2026. However, council notes: 'The KPI revision process took longer than originally anticipated; the delays are likely to impact the timely delivery of the revised performance reports and diminish scope for any corrective action that may be necessary.'
findings.matters: KPIs are the early-warning system for procurement control failures. Delayed reporting compresses the window for detecting and correcting problems before they escalate.
findings.quote: The KPI revision process took longer than originally anticipated; the delays are likely to impact the timely delivery of the revised performance reports and diminish scope for any corrective action that may be necessary.
